ext.research_question: Does out-group cueing from Democratic elites, delivered through news coverage, drive the rise of climate skepticism in the US public, especially among Republicans, and can that effect be shown to be causal rather than a by-product of confounders?
ext.theory: Elite cueing and out-group backlash. Partisans use party elites as cognitive shortcuts and affective anchors (Cohen 2003; Kam 2005; Lenz 2012; Lodge and Taber 2013). Out-group cues can repel rather than persuade partisans, plausibly via affective polarization (Iyengar et al. 2012). The authors contrast this with motivated-reasoning and ideology accounts, which they say cannot easily explain the over-time dynamics, since Republicans once matched Democrats on climate beliefs. News media carry elite cues to the mass public (pp. 2-6). Hypotheses: H1, Democratic elite cues lead aggregate skepticism; H2, a positive contemporaneous correlation holds after controls; H3, exposure to a Democratic cue raises skepticism among Republicans (pp. 5-8).
ext.data: Aggregate opinion: about 172 Roper Center poll questions (the abstract says "nearly 200 polls") combined into a latent skepticism index. Quarterly 2001-2014 (N=55 in Table 2 Model 1; N=54 for the Republican series) and annual 1986-2014 (N=28). Republican-only series is the Partisan Climate Change Threat Index of Carmichael and Brulle, reverse-coded (correlation 0.48 with the authors' quarterly series). News: climate coverage in the New York Times and Washington Post (LexisNexis), with 1,000+ articles hand-screened for relevance. Validation: 700 party-referencing articles (about 80% contain a cue); 3,000 articles coded for stance (97% of Democratic-cue articles fully pro-consensus); 2,179 newspaper articles coded for economic-cost and uncertainty frames (classifier training sets of 1,878 and 1,179). Experiment: MTurk, 2019, N=2,970 analysed (condition sizes 471-534), with 85% passing screeners and 130 (4%) dropped for failing both (p. 19 and fn 10).
ext.method: Text-as-data pipeline: Lexicoder plus a custom dictionary of party names, office titles and leaders to flag elite cues. Share of articles with Democratic cues and Republican cues. Republican cue measure is the cue share multiplied by the share of hostile Republican messages (validated against LCV scores, r=0.72). Frames via SVM (80% accuracy for cost frames, recall 0.76 and precision 0.80; 77% accuracy for uncertainty frames, recall 0.70 and precision 0.68). Time series: reduced-form VAR with lags up to four quarters (higher lag chosen when tests disagree; stability checked) and Granger causality tests, with controls for NOAA climate index, oil prices, unemployment and quarter dummies (pp. 11-13). Contemporaneous models: lagged-dependent-variable OLS with robust SEs (Eq. 1), controls for Republican cues, uncertainty and cost frames, salience (NYT plus WaPo volume), climate, oil, unemployment (Table 2). Experiment: OLS (Eq. 2) interacting five treatment dummies (Democratic cue; opposing GOP cue; polarized cues; supporting GOP cue; consensus cues) with 7-point partisanship and with controls (trust in scientists, political interest) and their interactions with treatment. Outcome is a 7-point agree/disagree item on human-caused warming, rescaled 0-1 (pp. 18-21).
ext.identification: Time series: Granger tests establish temporal precedence only, and the authors state the design is not causal (pp. 6, 12, 17). Contemporaneous models add controls for in-group cues, frames, salience, and lagged skepticism, but remain observational. Experiment: random assignment to six conditions (control; Democratic cue; opposing GOP cue; polarized; supporting GOP cue; consensus), so the cue effect is identified within the randomized conditions. Partisanship is not randomized and enters as a moderator (p. 19). The effects reported are conditional on strong partisanship. Effects are estimated through the PID-by-treatment interaction, not a simple randomized mean difference.
ext.scope: Population: US public (aggregate polls) and a US online MTurk sample (2019) that the authors say matches the public on gender, race, partisanship and ideology but skews younger, wealthier and more educated (p. 18). Institution: national newspaper coverage (NYT and WaPo) only. Era: 1986-2014 for annual opinion and 2001-2014 for quarterly series; experiment in 2019. Issue: climate change science and mitigation.

key_findings.finding: Democratic elite cues Granger-cause aggregate climate skepticism; the reverse does not hold.
key_findings.numbers: Dem cues -> skepticism chi2 6.96, p=0.01 (1 lag); skepticism -> Dem cues chi2 1.01, p=0.32

key_findings.finding: Democratic cues Granger-cause skepticism among Republicans; the reverse does not hold.
key_findings.numbers: Dem cues -> GOP skepticism chi2 7.35, p=0.03 (2 lags); GOP skepticism -> Dem cues chi2 0.29, p=0.86

key_findings.finding: Republican cues show weak and inconsistent cue-taking: no effect on aggregate skepticism, weak effect on Republican skepticism.
key_findings.numbers: GOP cues -> aggregate chi2 0.00, p=0.94; GOP cues -> GOP skepticism chi2 2.94, p=0.09; skepticism -> GOP cues p=0.82 and p=0.99

key_findings.finding: Contemporaneous association: Democratic cues correlate with aggregate skepticism after controls, weaker in the quarterly model.
key_findings.numbers: Quarterly coefficient 0.02 (SE 0.01), p~0.07; 10-point rise in Dem cue share = 0.2 SD in skepticism; N=55

key_findings.finding: Annual aggregate model shows the same association.
key_findings.numbers: Coefficient 0.02 (p~0.09); 10-point rise = 0.2 SD; R2=0.89; N=28. Republican cues not significant (p~0.60)

key_findings.finding: Republican-specific skepticism responds to Democratic cues (H2 support) and to Republican cues.
key_findings.numbers: Dem cues 0.03 (p<0.01) = 0.3 SD per 10 points; GOP cues 0.04 (p~0.02) = 0.4 SD per 10 points; N=54

key_findings.finding: Unemployment and salience also correlate with Republican skepticism; more coverage is associated with lower Republican skepticism after controls.
key_findings.numbers: 1-point unemployment rise = 0.3 SD (p<0.001); +100 articles per quarter = -0.4 SD (p~0.03)

key_findings.finding: Descriptive: Democratic cues track salience; Republican cues track economic-cost framing more than uncertainty framing.
key_findings.numbers: Dem cues vs salience 0.57 quarterly and 0.57 annual; Rep cues vs salience -0.45 and 0.11; Rep cues vs cost frames 0.64 quarterly and 0.55 annual; vs uncertainty 0.34 and -0.07

key_findings.finding: Democratic-cue articles are almost uniformly pro-consensus; Republican hostility to climate action is measured via a composite.
key_findings.numbers: 97% of Democratic-cue articles fully supportive of consensus (3,000-article hand-coded sample); cue screen validated at about 80% (700 articles); Rep composite correlates 0.72 with LCV scores; coder agreement alpha 0.98 (Dem), 0.83 (GOP)

key_findings.finding: Survey experiment: a Democratic elite cue polarizes strong Republicans toward skepticism (H3 support).
key_findings.numbers: Strong Republicans +0.06 on 0-1 scale (about 0.2 SD, p~0.03); interaction p~0.05. Strong Democrats: no significant effect

key_findings.finding: Opposing GOP cue and polarized cues (Democratic plus opposing Republican) raise Republican skepticism; polarized effect is largest.
key_findings.numbers: Opposing GOP: +0.06 (p~0.02; interaction p~0.02). Polarized: +0.09 (about 0.3 SD, p~0.002; interaction p~0.003); strong Democrats +0.04 (p~0.09)

key_findings.finding: Supporting GOP cue and consensus cue (Democratic plus supportive Republican) produce no polarization; the consensus cue attenuates the Democratic backlash.
key_findings.numbers: No significant effect for supporting GOP or consensus conditions; no depolarizing effect reported

key_findings.finding: Control condition baseline: 80% of respondents agree with the consensus at some level and 13% disagree.
key_findings.numbers: 80% agree at some level; 13% disagree; scale rescaled 0-1

limitations: VAR and Granger analyses cannot speak to contemporaneous relationships or causality; authors say so (pp. 6, 12, 16).
Aggregate evidence is described as only suggestive; unmeasured confounders over time remain (p. 17).
Results are sensitive to lag length; the authors pick the higher lag when tests disagree and note the sensitivity (fn 6, p. 12).
Small time series (N=28 annual, 54-55 quarterly) with many controls.
Cue measure is a share of articles from dictionary-based classification, not message volume; volume robustness is only in supplementary Table D1 (p. 10).

Republican hostility measure is a composite built from a 3,000-article coding and an LCV correlation (0.72); the authors call the stance indicator valid but it is not directly measured for every period (pp. 10-11).
Only NYT and WaPo are used; the authors acknowledge partisan online and social media are excluded (fn 3, p. 9).
Inconsistent counts: the abstract says nearly 200 polls, the body uses 172 poll questions (p. 8). The abstract says about 3,000 respondents; 2,970 were analysed.
Experimental sample is MTurk, skewing younger, wealthier and more educated; screeners address bot and VPN concerns (pp. 18-19, fn 10).
Partisanship is not randomized; treatment effects are moderated by PID, which may carry confounding (p. 19).
No effect among Democrats, possibly from a ceiling effect (p. 22).
Treatments are thin and the outcome is a single 7-point item (pp. 18-21).
Consensus cue did not depolarize; the authors suggest a stronger treatment from respected Republicans may be needed (p. 23).
Table 2 layout is hard to read: the text reports Model 1 Republican cues as non-significant, while the table marks Dem cues only with stars; p-values are reported as approximate (p~).

measures: Aggregate climate skepticism: latent, standardized index from about 172 Roper Center poll questions (annual 1986-2014; quarterly 2001-2014).
Republican climate skepticism: reverse-coded Partisan Climate Change Threat Index (Carmichael and Brulle 2017), quarterly from 2001.
Democratic elite cue share: share of NYT/WaPo climate articles with Democratic cues (Lexicoder plus dictionary).
Republican cue measure: share of cue articles x share of hostile Republican messages (composite; LCV r=0.72).
Uncertainty frame share and economic-cost frame share: SVM classifiers on hand-coded articles.
Salience: combined NYT and WaPo climate article volume.
Controls: NOAA climate index, oil prices, unemployment rate, quarter dummies, lagged dependent variable.
Experiment outcome: 7-point agreement that Earth is warming mostly due to human activity, rescaled 0-1.
Experiment moderator: 7-point partisanship (strong Democrat to strong Republican) and political interest and trust in scientists.

rel.summary_md:
Merkley and Stecula ask whether climate skepticism in the US public grew because people reacted against Democratic elites, with news coverage carrying those cues. They combine three methods. First, a Lexicoder dictionary flags party cues in NYT and WaPo climate coverage. Second, they run time-series models on a latent skepticism index built from about 172 poll questions. Third, they run a 2019 MTurk experiment with N=2,970.

In the time series, the share of articles carrying Democratic cues Granger-causes skepticism, both in the aggregate (chi2 6.96, p=0.01) and among Republicans (chi2 7.35, p=0.03). The reverse direction does not hold. Republican cues have no aggregate effect (p=0.94). In the experiment, a single Democratic cue moves strong Republicans +0.06 toward skepticism on a 0-1 scale (about 0.2 SD). A polarized cue, Democrats for and Republicans against, moves them +0.09. A consensus cue, with Republicans joining Democrats, produces no movement and does not depolarize. More coverage alone, with cues held fixed, goes with lower Republican skepticism (-0.4 SD per +100 articles a quarter). The Granger tests show only which series moves first, not causation. The causal evidence is one MTurk experiment on mass partisans, not legislators.

For Melange, the paper's value is about direction. An out-party cue is not a weaker positive cue. Among mass partisans it pushes the other way. Three parts of the engine encode out-party cues differently:
- The cascade kernel's cpf_pressure gives an out-party source 0.5x pull, a weaker push in the same direction.
- The LT-priming cross-cue is clamped at 0 and never goes negative.
- The salience shock already has a Retreat regime that moves out-partisans -1, but its Rally regime still gives bridge-builders +0.5. The paper's consensus condition found no movement at all.

The paper does not supply a legislator-level backfire magnitude. Every transfer runs from the mass public to members of Congress and from climate to credit-union issues, so any recalibration is UNVERIFIED and remains Paul's decision.

bearings.paper_claim: A polarized cue (Democrats for, Republicans against) moves strong Republicans +0.09 on a 0-1 scale (about 0.3 SD, p~0.002), the largest effect. A single Democratic cue moves them +0.06 (p~0.03). A consensus cue (Democrats plus supportive Republicans) produces no significant movement and no depolarization. In observational data, coverage volume with cues held fixed goes with LOWER Republican skepticism (-0.4 SD per +100 articles a quarter, p~0.03), so salience by itself is not what polarizes. Who is attributed the message is.
bearings.paper_location: Experimental results, Figure 3 Panels A-C, pp. 20-21; Table 2 Model 3, p. 17; discussion pp. 22-23
bearings.system_side: Going public is modelled as three regimes. Retreat moves co-partisans +1 and out-partisans -1, which matches the paper's polarized-cue backlash. Rally moves out-partisans +0.5 when bpf >= 0.30, which this paper's consensus null does not support. The regime probabilities p and q come from the current D-R tier gap z, a snapshot that the campaign itself never changes, and the actor's party defaults to R in the advisory.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over only as a direction-of-effect prior. The paper studies mass partisans responding to elite cues in national newspapers on climate, an issue with a large partisan gap; the engine moves legislators' stance tiers on credit-union issues. The rally result is a single thin MTurk treatment, so it weakens the case for out-partisan rally movement but does not refute it. The Granger evidence that Democratic cues come before Republican skepticism suggests z is endogenous to going public, but the paper estimates nothing that could calibrate that effect.

bearings.paper_claim: Out-group (Democratic) elite cues move Republicans away from the cued position rather than toward it. Experiment: strong Republicans +0.06 toward skepticism (about 0.2 SD, p~0.03), with a PID interaction p~0.05. Time series: Democratic cues Granger-cause Republican skepticism (chi2 7.35, p=0.03, 2 lags); the reverse has p=0.86.
bearings.paper_location: Table 1, p. 15; Figure 3 Panel A, p. 20
bearings.system_side: The Bakker cross-cue factor passes a cross-party pro-cue through sqrt(bpf_u*bpf_v), so a non-bridge out-party cue falls to about 0. It is clamped at 0 and never goes negative, and the code comment says 'backfire magnitude not invented'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper backs the claim that out-party cues do not persuade, and it suggests the true sign can be negative. Its +0.06 effect is measured on mass Republicans and a single climate item, not on legislators reading cosponsorship signals. It therefore cannot justify a negative magnitude for the priming term. Keeping the 0 clamp remains defensible.

bearings.paper_claim: In both the experiment and the time series, an out-party elite cue triggers backlash, not attenuated persuasion. Republican cues had no aggregate effect (chi2 0.00, p=0.94) and only a weak effect on Republican skepticism (p~0.09).
bearings.paper_location: Table 1, p. 15; Figure 3, p. 20; discussion p. 22
bearings.system_side: cpf_pressure gives an out-partisan source a positive 0.5x pull and a co-partisan source 1.7x. cpf_diffusion keeps a 0.4 cross-party floor. Both still treat out-party influence as weaker but same-signed.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper agrees that co-partisan sources dominate, which fits the 1.7/0.5 ordering. On issues as polarized as climate in the mass public, it puts the out-partisan sign at or below zero, not 0.5. The kernel runs on legislator cosponsorship ties, where out-party cosponsorship is an observed behaviour, not a cue, so transfer is weak. The paper gives no support for the 1.7/0.5 ratio itself.

bearings.paper_claim: The authors use Lexicoder plus a custom dictionary of party names, offices and leaders to detect who is cued, not sentiment. They validate it against hand coding of 700 articles (about 80% of flagged articles contain a real cue). Stance is hand-coded separately (97% of Democratic-cue articles fully pro-consensus), and frames come from SVMs (77-80% accuracy).
bearings.system_side: stage5_lsd.R runs the LSD2015 sentiment dictionary and computes tone intensity as charge per word. That intensity multiplies the stance sign in press_value.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Paul highlighted the Lexicoder use, but the paper validates the dictionary only for detecting actor references and never uses or validates LSD sentiment as an intensity measure. It is a method precedent for running dictionaries plus a hand-coded validation sample. It is not evidence that LSD tone intensity is valid on congressional press releases.

gaps_exposed: The engine never lets a source's party identity produce a negative cue. The cascade kernel, LT priming and the rally regime all keep out-party influence at zero or above. The only negative out-party movement is the salience shock's Retreat and Backfire regimes, and it never feeds the cascade kernel.

The salience shock takes partisan polarization (z) as a fixed snapshot of the stance matrix. Nothing models a CU campaign led by one party creating or widening the partisan gap over later quarters, which is the dynamic the Granger results describe.

Message attribution, meaning which party's elites are seen as owning a CU issue in press and news, is not measured. The frame-alignment and press layers measure duplication and stance, not attribution of party cues in third-party coverage.
The salience shock has no consensus regime. The paper's consensus condition (both parties supportive) is a distinct case with a null effect, not a rally that moves out-partisans +0.5.
flags: The paper's aggregate contemporaneous coefficient (0.02, p~0.07 quarterly; p~0.09 annual) pools Democrats and Republicans across the partisan fault line the paper is about. If quoted, label it UNSTRATIFIED and pair it with the Republican-only Model 3 (0.03, p<0.01, N=54, quarterly 2001-2014).
The Granger results depend on lag choice (the authors take the higher lag when tests disagree, fn 6). Quote them as evidence of which series moves first, never as causal.

Any proposal to give out-partisan pressure a negative sign, or to set a backfire magnitude in lt_priming, from the +0.06 or +0.09 MTurk effects would be new agent analysis, UNVERIFIED (DE-062). Those effects are mass-public climate effects and say nothing about legislators.
No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals, D-021 or D-025. The paper argues for neither dropping cosponsorship edges nor per-edge volume normalization.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's highlights match the paper's core claim (Democratic cues, Republican backlash, consensus cues fail). His component notes list Merkley and Stecula as support for treating party as a filter on receptiveness (cascade kernel) and as a companion to Noble and Turner (salience shock). The evidence agrees on direction but is stronger than the system as built. The paper finds that out-party cues backfire. In the code, out-party influence is attenuated but positive in cpf_pressure and the rally regime, and clamped at 0 in LT priming. So Paul's note is consistent with the system but understates the gap: the system handles backfire only through the salience shock's Retreat and Backfire regimes. His highlight of the Lexicoder method under lsd-tone is a loose fit. The paper used Lexicoder to detect party actors, not to measure tone, so it does not validate the LSD intensity the system uses. His closing highlights on cross-partisan elite consensus are tempered by the paper's own null for the consensus condition.

related.why: Noble and Turner supply the rally, retreat and backfire structure the salience shock implements. Merkley and Stecula give mass-public experimental evidence that the out-partisan retreat direction is real, and that a consensus or rally cue does not move out-partisans.

Bakker et al. is the cited basis for the LT-priming cross-cue clamp, which treats out-party cues as having null-to-backfire effects. Merkley and Stecula independently find backfire from out-party cues, on climate and in a news setting.

Both papers study cue-taking. Box-Steffensmeier et al. look at legislators taking cues from interest-group Dear Colleague letters. Merkley and Stecula look at the mass public taking cues from party elites in the news. Together they mark the boundary between legislator and voter evidence for the cue parameters.

Both rely on dictionaries for political text. Rice and Zorn argue that general-purpose sentiment dictionaries need adaptation to specialized vocabularies, which bears on applying LSD2015 to congressional releases. Merkley and Stecula use Lexicoder only with a custom dictionary validated against hand coding.

Haselmayer and Jenny also pair dictionary-based measurement of political communication with human validation (crowdcoding). That is the validation step the paper models and the system's LSD tone layer lacks.
